cases.chapter_title: 2. Public Comment. The City Council invites citizens to address the City Council on any matter, including items on the agenda, except public hearings that are included on the agenda. Comments related to Public Hearings will be heard when the specific hearing starts. Citizen comments are limited to three (3) minutes, unless otherwise required by law. To address the Council, please fill out a City Council Appearance Card and submit it to a staff member prior to the Public Comment item on the agenda. The Council is not permitted to take any action or discuss any item not listed on the agenda. The Council may choose to place the item on a future agenda.

To address the Council, please fill out a City Council Appearance Card and submit it to a staff member prior to the Public Comment item on the agenda. The Council is not permitted to take any action or discuss any item not listed on the agenda. The Council may choose to place the item on a future agenda.

Thank you for the way this meeting was conducted.
Thank you for the way everyone conducted themselves today, and I appreciate that.

And we are going to talk about the 2017 proposed budget.
Now, why don't we take a five-minute break?
We have been sitting a while.
I'm going to call us back to order, and we're going to go into our work session item, the 2017 proposed budget.
Mayor and Council, at the last council meeting, you all had asked a couple of questions regarding various things that were in the proposed budget.
So we have a few folks to come up and highlight a little more detail on some of the things you inquired about.
But then we'd also like to know if there's any other things that you're interested in.
We'd like to discuss during this budget process that we can get more information to you as we develop this over the weeks ahead.
So I think, let's see, planning, John, are you doing that?
So one of the questions you all talked about was the Neighborhood Matching Grant.
There is some provision of funding here.
And so John's going to talk a little bit about where we have been and kind of what's in the budget as it relates to the grant program.
This is one of those programs that's a feel-good program, and it actually does really good work for community development in the city.
It resonates well in neighborhoods, and it really doesn't cost a lot.
And it has some matching local funds really buy-in by the neighborhood.
So it has a lot of positive benefits all the way around.
Typical projects include entryways, signage, sign toppers, landscaping, some fencing, neighborhood capacity building to get people engaged.
And the grant program began back in 2007.
About $300,000 was spent up to 2012 on over 50 projects.

Uh, so some of the proposed regulations that staff is recommending is to update the Unified Development Code with the following.

transcript_excerpt.text: It just means that you're a body that makes recommendations to the city council,
and it's up to us to make the final decision.
And the difference in us and you is the fact that when we push the button and reach a decision, then that's it.
I mean, that comes back as being the facts.
And it's not something that anybody should fret over a second because we're all nine individuals like you all are
But it does mean that the system works the way it should work
and that we have two sets of – well, we have 18 sets of eyes that look on every case.
And none of those eyes are more important than others.
It just so happens that the city council has the option of voting something up or down and that's it.
So I don't know if that's been a source of irritation.
It was with the council that we had – I mean, the PNZ we had several years ago.
They had a difficult time with that – with us changing their decisions.
But that's what it's all about.
I tell you, I look through the hearings very carefully.
Some of the city council watches PNZ.
But I do read all the comments that you've made, and I think they're good comments.
I think you've done a great job and will continue to do a good job.
But Victor and I thought it would be good for all of us to get together
and talk about the vision of the council, the council priorities,
and things like that that you may not know firsthand.
So that's what this is about today.
I want it to be open and free.
I don't want to talk about any cases.
You know, one of those cases that we turned down that you approved, it's history,
so there's no reason going through that.
So, Victor, why don't you say a few words?
I'm delighted that we get a chance to sit with the city council.
It's a real privilege to serve with the people that I do,
and this has been something we've looked forward to for a while,
and everybody's schedule is tight and busy.
So, again, we're very appreciative of that.
We know that we serve as an advisory body to the city council.
You are the elected officials and, therefore, set the vision for the city
and you're accountable to the voters.
So you're the ones that need to have that final say.
And I think for us, they're probably in some specific areas that we'd certainly like to make sure,
just periodically, this being one of those times,
that we're reinforced with what the vision of the council is with respect to some specific topics.
We, as I think we've had it drilled into us, I've certainly espoused this as my philosophy,
and I think it's the council's philosophy, excuse me, the P&C commission's philosophy,
is that really we're guided by state law, city ordinance, and council vision.
And the laws and the ordinances are fairly dry at the moment.
I mean, they're fairly structured, and they're obviously changing over time as bodies look at them,
But the vision is the fluid thing, and that's really important to us to get the chance to hear from you.
So thank you for letting us be here.
I want council to correct me now if I say something that you don't think is true.
We haven't discussed the format for this meeting.
But talking about the council vision, let me just cover three areas that I believe we would all agree is a strong vision of the council.
One is the land use decision.
You know, we need a good balance of residential and commercial use.
And I think our goal, I think we would agree, the goal would be to have 60%, 70% of our land use commercial at this point.
Would you agree with that, council?
We're really strong in trying to build our commercial tax base.
You know, the residential and the commercial have not come close together.
Residential is always on top, way on top, which means you pay more taxes than you would if it were reversed.
Obviously, we want higher value housing.
Right now, the median house value in Arlington is about $130,000, $131,000, which is the lowest in the Metroplex.
And so we're after quality housing if we're talking about residential.
We love, as you do, probably mixed-use projects like Viridian, if it gets off the ground, like Glory Park, which I know some don't believe is going to happen.
I do believe it's going to happen in some fashion.
I'm not sure it's going to be a heavy retail use, but I believe it will happen.
We need higher value hotel construction.
You know, the council wisely passed an ordinance that would no longer allow limited service hotels to build in Arlington, although there's one big one that just built.

cases.chapter_title: 3. Public Comment. The City Council invites citizens to address the City Council on any matter, including items on the agenda, except public hearings that are included on the agenda. Comments related to Public Hearings will be heard when the specific hearing starts. Citizen comments are limited to three (3) minutes, unless otherwise required by law. To address the Council, please fill out a City Council Appearance Card and submit it to a staff member prior to the Public Comment item on the agenda. The Council is not permitted to take any action or discuss any item not listed on the agenda. The Council may choose to place the item on a future agenda.

a. Present, discuss, and consider action on an Ordinance ordering an election to be held in and throughout the Town of Addison, Texas, on May 2, 2026, to dissolve the Dallas Area Rapid Transit System (DART) in the Town of Addison, Texas, subject to the continued collection of sales taxes for the period required by law; providing for location of polling places to be designated at a later date; providing for early voting; and providing an effective date.

Good afternoon, Mayor and Council, Alicia Winkleback, Transportation Director.

We've been working hard to make sure that our residents and our visitors understand the different options we provide.
You've heard the city manager say numerous times that Uber and Lyft have solved the transportation problem,

What we're offering are lower cost subsidized options for our residents and visitors.

both of which are subsidized with both federal transit administration dollars
and then general fund dollars from the city.

which Ann will talk a little bit more about in a little while, and that's in partnership with TCC and UTA,
and we have some federal grant dollars we use, our $2 HandyTran fare,

transcript_excerpt.text: I ride a lot around Fort Worth, Dallas, Irving, Garland, Texas, and I see that dark bus, 2 o'clock in the afternoon, Sunday, nobody in there.
I went out to TRE Saturday, nobody in there.
I went to Irving on the regular day and watched the bus, I see two people in there.
You know, like I see the manager, we don't want to put in one penny, pay $100 million, and we have to cut all kinds of programs.
So I want the citizens of Arlington fully aware that we do have public transportation.
Is it the best we've got?
And I used it about a year ago, and I ride it at least six to eight times.
And I don't have any problem.
And this year, they gave me two free pass.
I didn't want to use it, because that cost the city money, so I didn't use it.
So, like I said, we do have public transportation.
I want the people of Citizen Arlington, watch this meeting today, know that we do have it.
And if they come up with the best solution, to show me, sit down and show me, and then I can bring it up to council member.
We're going to discuss that and make it better.
And thank you to you and your staff for the great job that you've done with the Nivea and the Handy Train.
And thank you to Ann and Alicia for all the work you do and for providing this service to our citizens.
Now we'll discuss our informal staff reports.
You've received written reports on the items listed below.
For the sake of time, staff will address specific questions you have.
I guess this is an attorney question.

With regards to that license agreement, if we can get out of it for any reason, how would that affect UTA, you know, since they're going to be in, you know, if the city decides to get out of it for some reason?
Would they still be able to do what they need to do?
So, Jana Wenzel, principal planner with the transportation department.
I just want to take a moment to let you know that we have representatives from UTA, VO, and downtown Arlington Management Corporation.
So, if the city were to withdraw from the license agreement and terminate it, scooters and bikes would only be allowed to operate on the UTA campus.
And the reason I ask that question, I mean, people have heard me before, and everywhere I go, I still see those scooters.
People don't ride them the way they're supposed to.
So, it's not anything to do with UTA or the city.
It's just the citizens that use them.
It's just, I think some of my fellow council members have gone, when we go to different conferences, they've commented to me.
It's like, you're right, look at this.
So, I'm really, like I said, I'm really concerned for the safety of our citizens and enforcement.
You know, we can't ride them on Cooper, but there's more and more on Cooper, and the students going up and down.

and improved pedestrian and bike safety infrastructure.
So, the team is going to be finalizing the draft document.

I would recommend that you table it.
So, recommend you make a motion to table.
Let me mark that on my copy.
Do we have anything else on the agenda?
I would like the staff to look into creating an office of energy efficiency and or sustainability
with a director, staff, so forth.
And as part of that, I'd like to research if other cities have done this.
And if they have, have they resulted in cost savings or, you know, what is the return on
that investment versus having that department?
Alternate to that, having a similar thing created within the city departments that already exist, just how much money can be saved
by looking into energy conservation efforts.
That's what I – I think that there have been some missed opportunities in the past,
and maybe that's because we don't have an advocate for those things or people just don't think about it.
Example is when we do a large project, city project, that's on a large piece of land,
we could have included geothermal possibilities in the request for proposal.
Perhaps if we had an advocate for that, that would have been included.
There's quite a few other examples.
So I'd like to get some kind of idea what that would cost versus possible benefits.

And during the time with our FSS program, she ended up with a pretty lucrative career, ended up getting her degree.
And then she used her escrow to purchase a home and is now no longer needing housing assistance.
So that's what our family self-sufficiency program does.
And then I want to talk about the other end of the spectrum, our homeless programs.
Here we have our homeless system, as you can see.
Partnership Home is our Continuum of Care lead agency, formerly Tarrant County Homeless Coalition.
They oversee the community plan to organize housing and services for the homeless in Tarrant and Parker County.
They also oversee the annual point-in-time count, that is the third Thursday of January, so that we can count all the homeless who are in shelter and unsheltered in Tarrant and Parker counties.
This helps us identify who's homeless, where are they, and that translates into homeless funding for our communities.

Partnership Home also oversees our coordinated entry process, which is designed to ensure those experiencing homeless are quickly identified, assessed, and served with the most appropriate housing intervention.
And just some of the programs that we have and offer at the Housing Authority, we have our Permanent Supportive Housing Program, which is long-term rental assistance.
That is for those who are disabled and chronically homeless, meaning they're disabled and they've been homeless for a year or more, or they've had four episodes within the last three years.
We're able to serve up to 32 households with this program, and we partner with MHMR of Tarrant County and Recovery Resource Council to provide supportive services for these folks.
We also have short-term rental assistance through our Rapid Rehousing.
That provides 12 to 24 months of rental assistance.
We provide the case management in-house for that program.
We're able to serve up to 19 households, and looks like we're going to have around $376,000 for our upcoming year budget for that program.

And then I want to talk about the other end of the spectrum, our homeless programs.
Here we have our homeless system, as you can see.
Partnership Home is our Continuum of Care lead agency, formerly Tarrant County Homeless Coalition.
They oversee the community plan to organize housing and services for the homeless in Tarrant and Parker County.
They also oversee the annual point-in-time count, that is the third Thursday of January, so that we can count all the homeless who are in shelter and unsheltered in Tarrant and Parker counties.
This helps us identify who's homeless, where are they, and that translates into homeless funding for our communities.

Partnership Home also oversees our coordinated entry process, which is designed to ensure those experiencing homeless are quickly identified, assessed, and served with the most appropriate housing intervention.
And just some of the programs that we have and offer at the Housing Authority, we have our Permanent Supportive Housing Program, which is long-term rental assistance.
That is for those who are disabled and chronically homeless, meaning they're disabled and they've been homeless for a year or more, or they've had four episodes within the last three years.
We're able to serve up to 32 households with this program, and we partner with MHMR of Tarrant County and Recovery Resource Council to provide supportive services for these folks.
We also have short-term rental assistance through our Rapid Rehousing.
That provides 12 to 24 months of rental assistance.
We provide the case management in-house for that program.
